source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET)
finding: Builds a semantic knowledge network of quantum physics: nodes are concepts, an edge means two concepts appear together in a paper. Tracks its growth over time.
numbers: 6,368 concept vertices; over 1.7 million edges from more than 15 million concept pairs; 750,000 papers, 1919 to Dec 2017; concepts extracted with RAKE plus filtering.
limits: Co-mention is a weak proxy for a real scientific link. One discipline only (quantum physics).
agent_relevance: A concept-pair graph is a cheap, auditable memory. Edges say what was studied together, so missing edges are the gaps.

source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET)
finding: Frames idea generation as link prediction: rank all unconnected concept pairs by chance of becoming connected within 5 years. A small neural net (4 fully connected layers) on 17 hand-built network features.
numbers: Only about 5% of possible pairs are connected by end of 2017. Trained on pre-2002 data to predict links by 2007, applied to 2007 data, validated on 2012 data never seen in training.
limits: Pairs sharing 20% or more of their neighbours were excluded so the task is not trivially similar terms. Co-occurrence is not impact.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable target for 'which unexplored link is worth trying': a held-out future-year test, in line with G3.

source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET)
finding: Prediction of new links works well on unseen future years.
numbers: AUC 0.85 for the 2017 network state (random = 0.5), 5-year horizon. Example pair with 22.8% shared neighbours became linked two years later.
limits: Single field; AUC rewards ranking, not whether the top pairs are interesting or true.
agent_relevance: A simple feature model on graph structure beats chance by a wide margin; a scaffold can use neighbourhood overlap as a retrieval signal.

source: Krenn & Zeilinger (2020) Predicting research trends with semantic and neural networks (SEMNET)
finding: Network growth tracking finds emerging fields: qubit (first appears 1995) and graphene-related concepts (from 2005, before the 2010 Nobel Prize) are among the fastest-growing concepts in the 5 years after first appearance.
numbers: Growth measured as number of papers mentioning a concept or pair in the first 5 years after first appearance, 1987 to 2017.
limits: Descriptive and retrospective; no test of causal effect.
agent_relevance: Growth after first linking is a usable 'this gap was fruitful' signal for ranking candidate links.

source: Gu & Krenn (2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics via machine learning on evolving knowledge graphs
finding: Extends link prediction from 'will be studied' to 'will be cited'. Builds a knowledge graph with a semantic layer (concept pairs from paper text) and an impact layer (citations).
numbers: Over 368,000 concepts; focus subgraph of 37,960 vertices and more than 26 million edges from 190 million concept pairs; 21 million papers; OpenAlex, data cutoff April 2023.
limits: Citation counts are a noisy impact measure; subfield is optics and quantum physics (about 10% of concepts).
agent_relevance: A candidate link can be scored for likely value, not only likelihood. Shows a graph memory can carry a payoff signal.

source: Gu & Krenn (2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics via machine learning on evolving knowledge graphs
finding: Predicts whether currently unconnected pairs will exist 3 years later; most settings reach very high AUC. Four model types (fully connected NN, Transformer, random forest, XGBoost) land within about 0.01 of each other.
numbers: 141 features per pair (41 network features). AUC about 0.93 to 0.98 across horizons and impact thresholds (e.g. fcNN 0.9631, Transformer 0.9571, forest 0.9532, XGBoost 0.9599 in one panel); random = 0.5.
limits: Easy negatives dominate the unconnected set; AUC overstates precision at the top of the ranking.
agent_relevance: Model family barely matters; features from graph structure carry the signal.

source: Gu & Krenn (2025) Forecasting high-impact research topics via machine learning on evolving knowledge graphs
finding: Genuine impact prediction is harder than link prediction. Train on unconnected pairs from 2016, evaluate on pairs from 2019 with outcomes checked in 2022 (never trained on 2019 to 2022).
numbers: For the harder task (low citation vs at least 100): AUC above 0.7 on test and above 0.67 on evaluation. Mean citations of top-ranked pairs far above the average of 0.029 citations over all 10^7 pairs.
limits: Drops from about 0.95 to about 0.69 once the target is impact. Pairs' citations are heavy-tailed.
agent_relevance: Warn: predicting 'will be connected' is not predicting 'will matter'. Do not treat link scores as value.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Uses a knowledge graph of papers as the retrieval memory for LLM idea generation. Retrieves 'inspirations' by three routes: semantic neighbours (SentenceBERT cosine), knowledge-graph neighbours, and citation neighbours.
numbers: Input from NLP and biomedical papers; 59k papers retrieved from; IE preprocessing precision 91% to 100% except relation extraction 65%; 79.7% of instances pass all steps.
limits: Ground truth ideas come from the same literature; retrieval quality caps results.
agent_relevance: A direct template for analogue retrieval: pull neighbouring and cited items, not only the most similar text.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: GPT-4 alone gives ideas of low technical depth and low novelty. In human comparison with ground truth ideas, the real idea wins nearly always.
numbers: In 85% of comparisons the ground-truth idea was judged to have significantly higher technical level and novelty; rest ambiguous. GPT4 few-shot plus KG neighbours had higher technical detail in 48% of pairs and was less incremental in 45% vs plain few-shot GPT4.
limits: Small human study; annotator agreement on Study I was 43.8% to 75.0% by pair (Table 13).
agent_relevance: Retrieval from a graph helps but does not close the gap. Expect shallow recombination.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Iterative novelty boosting: compare the idea with retrieved prior work and rewrite until it is different enough. First round changes most ideas; second round still adds.
numbers: Study III, 70 instances, 5 annotators: 88.9% of ideas substantially different after round 1; 55.6% more novel after round 1; 57.8% of those continued were more novel after round 2. Novelty was not observed to drop.
limits: The authors say ideas are 'often superficial recombinations of common concepts'. Needs a retrieval model to say what already exists.
agent_relevance: Code can run 'is this already in memory?' and trigger a rewrite only on a hit, matching G1 (doubt on a signal).

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: The paper notes models tend to copy specific details directly from retrieved inspirations and produce generic suggestions.
numbers: Qualitative finding; GPT-based models were outperformed by T5 on automatic metrics but won in human evaluation.
limits: Automatic metrics and human judgement disagree.
agent_relevance: Copying from retrieved items is a known failure; check for overlap with retrieved text in code.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster & Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery. PNAS 112(47)
finding: Models science as a network of chemicals (nodes) and published relations (links). Problem choice depends on node importance (degree) and difficulty (network distance). Infers the strategy from millions of MEDLINE abstracts and patents over 30 years.
numbers: Strategy parameters fitted every 5 years 1975 to 2010 by simulated annealing and MCMC (about 2 weeks on a 24-core machine).
limits: Published links are an imperfect record of effort; authors flag that failures and publication bias distort it.
agent_relevance: The cleanest formal model of search over a knowledge graph: importance plus distance. A direct blueprint for scoring candidate links.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster & Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery. PNAS 112(47)
finding: Scientists mostly follow central, known nodes. Preference for central chemicals rises steadily over time; science becomes more conservative.
numbers: Most published links join chemicals already linked (distance 1). Most novel links join chemicals at distance 2 (triadic closure); disconnected pairs next; other distances extremely rare.
limits: Observational; cannot separate 'fewer risky projects' from 'fewer risky projects succeed'.
agent_relevance: Left alone, a retrieval-driven agent drifts to the hub nodes too. Add an explicit push to far-but-reachable pairs.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster & Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery. PNAS 112(47)
finding: The observed strategy is inefficient for uncovering a mature network. Simulations on a sample of the 2010 MEDLINE network show better strategies.
numbers: MEDLINE strategy is most efficient at about 13% of the network discovered; over three times more costly than the best alternative for the bulk of the network; the best strategy for 50% coverage is nearly 10 times more efficient than random.
limits: A simulation on a sub-sampled network, not a field experiment.
agent_relevance: Exploit-heavy search is fine early and wasteful late. A budgeted agent should shift toward risk as local ground is covered.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster & Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery. PNAS 112(47)
finding: Prize winners and highly cited authors use more diverse strategies, mixing central and peripheral chemicals and bridging disconnected parts of the network.
numbers: Combinations of more and less central chemicals link to higher citations and awards (their Fig. S3A).
limits: Correlation; winners may be selected after the fact.
agent_relevance: Supports a mix of hub and periphery items when retrieving analogues.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky & Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies. Am. Sociol. Rev.
finding: Typology of moves on a chemical knowledge network: jump (new entities), new consolidation, new bridge, repeat consolidation, repeat bridge. The mix is stable over decades.
numbers: Period 1983 to 2008. Repeat statements were six times more frequent than new or jump statements (85.8% vs 14.2%). New bridges and consolidations vs jumps: 12.4% vs 1.8%.
limits: MEDLINE chemistry only; counts only what is published.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary for operator choices: extend a cluster, bridge two clusters, or jump to a new entity.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky & Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies. Am. Sociol. Rev.
finding: Risky moves pay more on average but not enough to offset the risk; rare strategies get more citations.
numbers: Rare strategies such as jumps and new consolidations get more citations (their Fig. 3); articles by winners of 137 prizes in biomedicine and chemistry are enriched for new chemicals and new relations.
limits: Expected reward still below the risk-adjusted level for ordinary scientists; explained by a gamble for extreme impact.
agent_relevance: Expected-value reasoning for an agent: reward for bridging is skewed, so run a few high-risk bridges rather than shifting all effort.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature. Nature 571
finding: Word2vec skip-gram on materials abstracts captures chemistry without labels. Vectors support domain analogies, e.g. ferromagnetic - NiFe + IrMn gives antiferromagnetic.
numbers: About 3.3 million abstracts (1922 to 2018, over 1,000 journals), 1.5 million kept as relevant by a classifier; vocabulary about 500,000 words; 200-dimensional embeddings.
limits: Removing irrelevant abstracts improved performance; corpus choice matters (Extended Data Table 4).
agent_relevance: Embedding distance is a soft version of graph proximity; useful for analogue retrieval across surface forms.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature. Nature 571
finding: Retrospective test of discovery: use only abstracts before a cutoff (2001 to 2018), rank materials by cosine to the word 'thermoelectric', check what is later reported as thermoelectric.
numbers: Top 50 predictions were on average 8 times more likely to be studied as thermoelectrics within 5 years than a random unstudied material, and 3 times more likely than a random material with non-zero DFT bandgap.
limits: 'Studied as thermoelectric' means co-mention with a keyword in an abstract, not verified performance. Later corpora gave better hit rates.
agent_relevance: Evidence that similarity in a text-derived space predicts future links, 8 times over chance. Check with held-out time splits.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature. Nature 571
finding: Case from the 2009 cutoff: one of the top five predictions, CuGaTe2, would have been ranked top five four years before its 2012 publication as a strong thermoelectric. Two others (ReS2, CdIn2Te4) were suggested in literature shortly after.
numbers: Top-5 ranking from abstracts before 2009; rank trace shown for later years.
limits: Anecdotal, hand-picked from a ranked list of 5.
agent_relevance: Illustrates 'latent knowledge': facts are in the text but unlinked in anyone's head. Useful as an argument for retrieval.

source: Tshitoyan et al. (2019) Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature. Nature 571
finding: Same embeddings, only the target word changes, also rank candidates for other properties (e.g. ferroelectrics, photovoltaics) without retraining.
numbers: Procedure is a dot product between material vector and property vector; no new training.
limits: Target property word must exist in the vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Cheap reuse of a stored representation: one memory, many queries.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review of ideas from a retrieval-augmented LLM agent vs 49 human experts' ideas. LLM ideas are rated more novel, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: Novelty score human 4.84 vs AI 5.64 vs AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p < 0.05); 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers. Feasibility 6.61 (human) vs 6.34 (AI) vs 6.44 (rerank), not significant. Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 vs 5.46.
limits: Novelty is hard for experts to judge; ideas not executed. The authors propose an execution study.
agent_relevance: LLM ideas pass as novel but may not be feasible; add a feasibility check by code or an executed test.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Generating at scale hits a diversity wall: most ideas are duplicates.
numbers: Out of 4,000 seed ideas only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.8 counts as duplicate; about 5% unique). Non-duplicate share per batch falls as generation continues.
limits: Duplicate threshold chosen by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: More samples from one model do not give independent ideas. Supports G4. Deduplicate in code.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: LLM self-evaluation of ideas is unreliable; the authors list it as an open problem next to lack of diversity.
numbers: Authors report 'failures of LLM self-evaluation' as one of two main open problems (the other is lack of diversity in generation).
limits: Specific agreement numbers for the ranker not extracted in this session.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model judge its own ideas; code or external checks select (G5).

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Adds people to the knowledge graph. A hypergraph links materials, properties and the researchers who study them; unsupervised embeddings then predict what is likely to be discovered next.
numbers: Up to 400% better precision than content-only models, especially when literature is sparse; about 100% gain over the Tshitoyan word2vec approach for materials discoveries.
limits: Tests on materials (thermoelectric, ferroelectric, photovoltaic) and drug repurposing; the predicted discoveries are those humans reach.
agent_relevance: Who studies what predicts what will be linked. For an agent: a source's neighbourhood includes who or what context used it.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Drug repurposing for COVID-19: precision of candidates later chosen by experts for trials.
numbers: Human-aware precision reached 42% by July 2021, which is 350 to 400% higher than content-only candidates (10% after 12 months, 12% in July 2021).
limits: The 12-month human-aware figure was not extracted separately.
agent_relevance: A graph that models attention beats one that models only content for short-run forecasting.

source: Sourati & Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Reverses the signal: choose hypotheses unlikely for the crowd. 'Alien' hypotheses are promising but not predicted to be pursued for years.
numbers: Intellectual arbitrage between isolated communities; authors say alien predictions outperform published discoveries in their tests.
limits: Evaluation by retrospective data; no prospective trial of alien hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Two modes: predict the crowd to find fast wins, avoid it to find novel ones. A schema can pick the mode on purpose.

source: Qi et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Zero Shot Hypothesis Proposers
finding: Biomedical hypothesis task with a time split. Training set before Jan 2023; unseen test set from Aug 2023, after the models' training data. A multi-agent framework with search tools is tested.
numbers: Three evaluators on 100 unseen examples; ChatGPT and human scores correlate (Pearson and Spearman above 0.7 for all models). Finding: raising uncertainty (collaborative agents) helps candidate generation.
limits: Judging by ChatGPT; small human sample; claims of 'validated' hypotheses rest on matching later literature.
agent_relevance: Time-split design avoids leakage. Use it to test any memory-retrieval claim.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Large Language Models for Automated Open-domain Scientific Hypotheses Discovery
finding: First dataset for social-science hypothesis discovery from raw web text; multi-module LLM framework with three feedback loops; claims LLMs can propose hypotheses not in prior literature.
numbers: Evaluation by GPT-4 and expert raters; exact scores not extracted in this session beyond the abstract and introduction.
limits: Only abstract and introduction were read for numbers.
agent_relevance: Use as a design pattern: observe, propose, check against literature, feed back.

source: Chu & Evans (2021) Slowed canonical progress in large fields of science. PNAS
finding: Large fields entrench: more papers do not turn over the central ideas; they ossify the canon.
numbers: 1.8 billion citations among 90 million papers across 241 subjects (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only; not read in full.
agent_relevance: Warns that a citation-weighted memory will reinforce the canon; cap hub weight in retrieval.

source: Swanson (1986) Fish oil, Raynaud's syndrome, and undiscovered public knowledge
finding: Founding case of literature-based discovery: two literatures with no shared citations, linked through intermediate terms (blood viscosity, platelet aggregation) to propose fish oil for Raynaud's syndrome.
numbers: Not opened; reported from memory.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Open/closed discovery A-B-C pattern is the oldest form of link prediction on a concept graph.

source: Fortunato et al. (2018) Science of science. Science 359
finding: Review that frames knowledge networks, atypical combinations, and the shape of discovery as core themes of the field.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Named key work for this subfield in SUBFIELDS.md.
